questions.q: What is the key difference between Windows Authentication mode and Mixed Mode?
options: Windows Authentication allows only Windows/AD-backed logins; Mixed Mode adds SQL Server logins with passwords SQL Server itself stores and validates
Mixed Mode is only available on Linux
Windows Authentication requires a password to be sent over the network
There is no real difference — both modes behave identically
questions.explain: Mixed Mode is additive: it keeps Windows Authentication and adds SQL Server logins whose passwords SQL Server manages directly.

questions.q: Why does Windows Authentication have a security edge over SQL logins, per this lesson?
options: No password is ever sent to SQL Server — Kerberos/NTLM prove identity and SQL Server just trusts the token
Windows Authentication is faster at query execution
Windows Authentication doesn't require any login object at all
SQL logins are always stored in plaintext by design
questions.explain: With Windows Authentication, identity is proven via Kerberos/NTLM without a password crossing the wire to SQL Server.

questions.q: What are the two real best practices this lesson gives for the sa account?
options: Disable it if nothing depends on it, or rename it and give it a long, random password if it must stay enabled
Always leave it enabled with the default password for compatibility
Delete the sa login entirely — SQL Server allows this
Grant it to every application service account
questions.explain: sa is a well-known, high-privilege target — disabling it (or renaming + strong password if required) reduces attack surface.

questions.q: When is Mixed Mode actually necessary, according to this lesson?
options: For non-domain applications, legacy clients, or cross-platform connections that can't use Windows Authentication
It's always required, in every SQL Server installation
Only when using SQL Server Express edition
Mixed Mode is never necessary under any circumstance
questions.explain: The lesson frames Mixed Mode as the exception, needed when a client genuinely can't authenticate via Windows/AD.

questions.q: Why does centralized management favor Windows Authentication, per this lesson?
options: Disabling an account in Active Directory instantly cuts off every SQL login tied to it
Active Directory has no effect on SQL Server logins
SQL logins are automatically synced to Active Directory
Centralized management only applies to Mixed Mode
questions.explain: Because Windows-backed logins are tied to AD identities, disabling the AD account immediately revokes SQL Server access too.
